FOX 13's Aaron Mesmer reports. The Brief Bay Area dengue fever cases jumped to 33 locally acquired infections as health officials issue countywide warnings. Hillsborough County Mosquito Management Services is launching aerial spray runs over South Tampa and Ybor City to stop transmission. Health officials urge residents to empty standing water around homes and follow basic mosquito defense steps. TAMPA, Fla. - Locally acquired dengue fever cases in the Bay Area have climbed to 33, prompting mosquito control agencies in Hillsborough and Pinellas counties to ramp up surveillance, inspections and spraying, according to the Florida Mosquito Control Association (FMCA). The FMCA said Monday that Florida has recorded more than 40 confirmed locally acquired dengue cases this year, including 30 in Hillsborough County and three in Pinellas County. Hillsborough and Pinellas counties are under mosquito-borne illness alerts from the Florida Department of Health. Bay Area dengue fever cases By the numbers: The latest cases represent a significant increase from the numbers reported earlier this summer, which included 10 locally-acquired cases that were reported in the Bay Area last month. PREVIOUS: Dengue fever: 10 locally-acquired cases reported in Tampa Bay Statewide, the locally acquired cases include: 30 in Hillsborough County Seven in Miami-Dade County Three in Pinellas County One in Palm Beach County That brings the statewide total to 41 confirmed locally acquired cases. In Hillsborough County, mosquito surveillance has also detected dengue virus in 10 mosquito pools, according to the FMCA. Locally acquired cases mean the virus was transmitted by mosquitoes in the area rather than being associated with travel. Dengue is mainly spread by infected Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, which are active during the day and can breed in very small amounts of standing water around homes. Hillsborough mosquito spraying Local perspective: Hillsborough County Mosquito Management Services said crews are increasing mosquito treatments by air and ground because mosquito traps in neighborhoods are showing dengue virus activity. The county previously planned aerial applications Monday night in the Seffner and Brandon areas. On Tuesday night, mosquito control crews will conduct additional aerial applications in South Tampa and Ybor City. The Hyde Park treatment is scheduled from 8:30 p.m. Tuesday through 6 a.m. Wednesday in an area bounded by I-275, Bayshore Boulevard and West Watrous Avenue, the Hillsborough River and Hillsborough Bay, and South Manhattan Avenue. The Ybor City treatment is scheduled between 4 and 6 a.m. Wednesday in an area bounded by I-4, the Lee Roy Selmon Expressway, North 39th Street and North Taliaferro Avenue. County officials said alternate spray dates are scheduled for Tuesday and Wednesday if weather or other conditions prevent the treatments. Residents can contact Hillsborough County Mosquito Management Services at 813-635-5400 for more information. Pinellas dengue response Dig deeper: Pinellas County Mosquito Control is also increasing its response as the number of locally acquired dengue cases grows across the Tampa Bay region. Crews are focusing on ground inspections and daytime fogging in Palm Harbor and St. Petersburg, while continuing surveillance and treatments throughout the county. Officials are also conducting door-to-door inspections to identify and eliminate mosquito breeding sites on private property. "Dengue does not stop at county lines," Pinellas County Mosquito Control Director Alissa Berro said. "The mosquitoes that transmit the virus generally stay within a relatively small area, but people travel throughout the Tampa Bay area every day. When someone infected with dengue enters a new area, a local mosquito can bite that person and later spread the virus to others. As cases rise across the region, so does the potential for additional local transmission in Pinellas County." Because the mosquitoes that spread dengue often breed on private property, officials say residents play an important role in reducing the risk of additional transmission. Protecting yourself from dengue What you can do: Health and mosquito control officials are urging residents to follow the 3 Ds: Dress: Wear light-colored, long-sleeved clothing and closed-toed shoes when outdoors. Defend: Use an insect repellent with a CDC-recommended ingredient, including DEET, picaridin, IR3535 or oil of lemon eucalyptus. Dump: Empty or cover standing water around homes, including water in buckets, toys, plant saucers, tires and other containers. Officials say mosquitoes can breed in extremely small amounts of water, making it important to regularly check yards and other outdoor areas. Dengue fever symptoms Why you should care: The FDOH says dengue can cause a flu-like illness with fever, severe muscle aches and joint pain and sometimes a rash. Symptoms can appear within about 15 days after a person is bitten by an infected mosquito. Dengue is not spread through ordinary person-to-person contact. Anyone experiencing symptoms should contact a health care provider and mention any potential exposure to mosquitoes. What they're saying: Peter Jiang, director of Hillsborough County Mosquito Management and president of the FMCA, said dengue can be debilitating and, in severe cases, life-threatening. The disease is sometimes called "break-bone fever" because of the intense muscle, joint and bone pain it can cause, according to Jiang. Mosquito control agencies are continuing to coordinate with the Florida Department of Health on surveillance, education and treatment as the number of cases is expected to increase in the state's upcoming weekly report. For Bay Area residents, officials say one of the most effective ways to help prevent further spread is to eliminate standing water around their homes while taking steps to prevent mosquito bites. The Source: The information in this story was gathered from official updates provided by the Florida Mosquito Control Association, Hillsborough County Mosquito Management Services, Pinellas County Mosquito Control, and the Florida Department of Health. content: Find us on Google 📌 America's birthday 🎂 Start the day smarter ☀️ Get the USA TODAY app U.S. Politics Sports Entertainment Life Money Travel Opinion Crossword ONLY AT USA TODAY: Newsletters For Subscribers Real Estate From the Archives USA TODAY PLAY Crossword Marvel Comics eNewspaper Magazines Investigations Video Podcasts Humankind Advertise Your Business WITNESS (True Crime) Just Curious Best-selling Booklist Top Workplaces Nomination Legals Press Releases Cars Grocery Shopping OUR PORTFOLIO: Real Estate 10BEST USA TODAY Store Shopping Blueprint WITNESS (True Crime) Southern Kitchen Home Internet Services STATE Dengue fever Add Topic Dengue surges in Florida with 18 new cases reported in one week Cheryl McCloud USA TODAY NETWORK - Florida Updated Aug. 31, 2026, 12:17 p.m. ET Hear this story Florida has reported 41 locally acquired dengue cases in 2026, with 18 new cases in a single week; Hillsborough County accounts for 30. Eight Florida counties are under mosquito-borne illness advisories or alerts, including Hillsborough, Miami-Dade, and Pinellas. FDOH recommends DEET-based repellents and a "drain and cover" strategy to reduce mosquito exposure at home. Cases of dengue continue to increase across Florida, with 18 new locally acquired cases reported in one week by the Florida Department of Health. That brings the statewide total of dengue cases to 41 for the year as of Aug. 22. ➤ Meet the mosquito, the world's deadliest animal The mosquito-borne illness is one of several monitored by the agency. Eight counties are under either a mosquito-borne illness advisory or mosquito-borne illness alert. Shop Amazon for mosquito repellents Here's what you should know about mosquito-borne illnesses in Florida, symptoms to watch for and how best to prevent mosquito bites. How many types of mosquito-borne illnesses are there in Florida? FDOH compiles weekly data on the following mosquito-borne viruses in a report called "Florida Arbovirus Surveillance": West Nile virus (WNV) Eastern equine encephalitis virus (EEEV) St. Louis encephalitis virus (SLEV) Dengue virus (DENV) Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) Zika virus (ZIKV) California encephalitis group viruses (CEV) Malaria Mosquito-borne illness alerts, advisories issued for these Florida counties A mosquito-borne illness advisory has been issued for the following counties: Alachua Leon Palm Beach Pasco Walton A mosquito-borne illness alert has been issued for the following counties: Hillsborough Miami-Dade Pinellas "A mosquito-borne illness advisory means the public should take precautions to reduce mosquito bites due to factors indicating local disease such as positive sentinels, very few presumptive or positive human cases, or other justifications," according to Sarasota County. "A mosquito-borne illness alert means that there has been heightened disease activity, a significant increase in vector (disease capable) mosquito populations, or an increase in locally-transmitted human cases. "Residents should continue to take precautions, but exercise additional caution in preventing mosquito bites." Is dengue spreading in Florida? See counties reporting mosquito-borne illnesses According to the Florida Department of Health, as of Aug. 22, there have been 41 cases of locally acquired cases of dengue reported, along with 2 cases of West Nile Virus: Dengue: 41 cases 30 in Hillsborough County 7 in Miami-Dade County 1 in Palm Beach County 3 in Pinellas County West Nile: 2 1 in Alachua County 1 in Walton County Dengue in Florida: What symptoms should you watch for? "Dengue fever can be a painful, debilitating disease but is rarely fatal," the Florida Department of Health said. Symptoms appear three to 14 days after the bite of an infected mosquito and include: sudden onset of fever severe headache eye pain muscle and joint pain (giving the disease the nickname “breakbone fever”) bleeding Gastrointestinal symptoms like vomiting and diarrhea may also be present in some cases. "Dengue fever symptoms usually lasts four to seven days. The disease is often diagnosed incorrectly because the symptoms are similar to influenza and other viruses." Is dengue contagious? Dengue is spread by mosquitoes. Mosquitoes become infected with dengue after biting a person with the virus. Those infected mosquitoes then spread the virus to other people through bites. The Centers for Disease Control said a woman who is infected with the dengue virus during pregnancy could pass the virus to her fetus, causing death to the fetus, low birth weight or premature birth. What are symptoms of West Nile virus? "West Nile virus is a mosquito-borne flavivirus that causes mild to severe illness," the Florida Department of Health said. "Approximately 80% of people who are infected with WNV will not show any symptoms at all." Mild symptoms include: fever headache body aches nausea vomiting Sometimes swollen lymph glands or a skin rash on the chest, stomach and back. Symptoms can last from a few days to several weeks. About one in 150 people infected with West Nile will develop severe illness. Symptoms include: high fever headache neck stiffness stupor disorientation coma tremors convulsions muscle weakness vision loss numbness paralysis "These symptoms may last several weeks, and neurological effects may be permanent. Severe illness can also result in death," FDOH said. "Zika symptoms usually last for several days to a week," FDOH said. "People usually do not get sick enough to go to the hospital. For this reason, many people might not realize they have been infected." What are the best mosquito repellents to use? According to the Florida Department of Health, repellents with the following active ingredients provide the best protection: DEET Picaridin IR3535 Oil of lemon eucalyptus Para-menthane-diol 2-undecanone, a plant-derived ingredient 'Drain and cover' helps keep mosquitoes away The FDOH offered this advice to help keep mosquitoes away from your Florida home: Drain Drain water from garbage cans, old tires, pool covers, or any other containers where water collects. Empty and clean birdbaths and pet water bowls at least once or twice a week. Protect boats and vehicles from rain with tarps that don’t accumulate water. Maintain swimming pools in good condition and ensure they are appropriately chlorinated. Empty plastic swimming pools when not in use. Cover If you must be outside when mosquitoes are active, cover up. Apply mosquito repellent to exposed skin and clothing. Use mosquito netting to protect children younger than 2 months old.
